games.title: Agon
games.tagline: Guide your Queen to the centre of a 91-hex board
games.how_to_play: Maneuver your Queen to the center hexagon and surround it with all six Guards. Pieces move one step to adjacent hexes, capturing by custodianship when flanking opponents on opposite sides.

games.title: Asalto
games.tagline: Officers defend a fortress against a siege of soldiers
games.how_to_play: Asymmetric Victorian-era game where a small defending force (the Officers) holds off a larger attacking force (the Soldiers) on a fortress-and-plain board.

variants.title: Royal Garrison
variants.win: Officers: reduce Soldiers below immobilizing threshold. Soldiers: immobilize all three Officers.
variants.special: Extended Asalto variant. Three Officers defend a larger fortress against 50 Soldiers. Mechanics identical to Standard Asalto; scale increases strategic complexity.

variants.title: Asalto (Standard)
variants.win: Officers: capture enough Soldiers that the remaining force cannot surround both Officers. Soldiers: immobilize both Officers.
variants.special: Asymmetric siege game. Officers jump to capture (like draughts); Soldiers advance forward or sideways without jumping. Soldiers win by immobilizing; Officers win by reducing the Soldier force below the critical threshold.

games.title: Backgammon
games.tagline: Five thousand years of race, risk, and probability
games.how_to_play: Roll dice and race your 15 pieces around the board, bearing them off before your opponent. Combine racing, blocking, hitting, and probability management with the doubling cube for betting.

variants.title: Standard Backgammon
variants.win: Bear off all 15 pieces before your opponent
variants.special: Doubling cube allows stakes to be raised during play. Hit pieces are sent to the bar.

variants.title: Nardi
variants.win: Bear off all 15 pieces before your opponent
variants.special: No hitting. Both players move in the same direction. No doubling cube.

variants.title: Acey-Deucey
variants.win: Bear off all 15 pieces before your opponent
variants.special: Rolling 1-2 grants any doublet of your choice plus another roll. Pieces enter from the bar one at a time.

variants.title: Plakoto
variants.win: Bear off all 15 pieces before your opponent
variants.special: Pin instead of hit: landing on a blot traps it under your piece. Trapped pieces cannot move until released.

variants.title: Fevga
variants.win: Bear off all 15 pieces before your opponent
variants.special: No blots allowed: a point with one of your pieces is immediately blocked to the opponent. No hitting.

variants.title: Hypergammon
variants.win: Bear off all 3 pieces before your opponent
variants.special: 3 pieces per side placed on the last three points. Games last 10–15 minutes. Fully solved by computer.

variants.title: Nackgammon
variants.win: Bear off all 15 pieces before your opponent
variants.special: 2 extra checkers placed on the 23-point create a slower, more complex opening than standard Backgammon.

variants.title: Chouette
variants.win: Accumulate the most points across multiple games as the box, or advance to become the box
variants.special: Multiplayer format: one player (the box) faces a team. The box rotates when they lose. Consultation rules vary.

games.title: Basic Roleplaying
games.tagline: The percentile-skill engine behind Call of Cthulhu, RuneQuest, and Pendragon
games.how_to_play: Roll percentile dice against your skill ratings to determine success. Characters are defined by characteristics (Strength, Dexterity, etc.) and skills, not classes. One player is GM, others are player characters.

games.title: Bavarian 32-Card Games
games.tagline: Trick-taking games for the 32-card Skat deck
games.how_to_play: The 32-card German deck (Skat deck) supports 2 games: Schafkopf and Skat. Both are trick-taking games with permanent trumps and card-point scoring.

games.title: Cairn
games.tagline: A classless OSR adventure game about exploring a dark and mysterious Wood
games.how_to_play: Roll 3d6 for attributes, equip yourself from a random background, then explore a dark Wood filled with monsters and treasure. Fiction-first resolution with saves only for risky moments.

games.title: Chaupar
games.tagline: The ancient Indian game of the Mahabharata — three long dice, super-pieces, and split throws
games.how_to_play: Team race game on a cross-shaped board. Roll three long dice, split the result among your pieces, and race to return all pieces to the center. Pieces combine into super-pieces for capture immunity.

variants.title: Chaupar (Standard)
variants.win: Both teammates return all their pieces to the Charkoni first, after capturing at least one opponent piece
variants.special: Three long dice. No grace rolls. No castle squares. Super-pieces immune to smaller groups.

games.title: Chess
games.tagline: Every chess variant, one engine
games.how_to_play: A unified platform for 155 chess variants spanning classic FIDE rules, asymmetric battles, hidden information, expanded boards, alternative win conditions, regional forms, and topology variants. Every variant shares the chess lineage but modifies setup, pieces, board, or victory condition.

variants.title: Alice Chess
variants.board: Two 8×8 boards (Board A and Board B)
variants.special: After every move, the moving piece transfers to the corresponding square on the other board. A move is only legal if the transfer square is vacant. Invented V. R. Parton, 1953.

variants.title: Standard Grasshopper Chess
variants.special: Each queen is replaced by a Grasshopper — a piece that must hop over a hurdle to move.

variants.title: Gygax Chess
variants.special: Three stacked 12×8 boards. 42 pieces per side across 15 piece types. Air, Land, and Subterranean realms. Gary Gygax, Dragon Magazine No. 100, 1985.

variants.title: Standard Nightrider Chess
variants.special: Knights are replaced by Nightriders — riders that chain knight-leaps in a single direction.

variants.title: Standard Chess
variants.special: Standard FIDE rules

variants.title: Standard Wildebeest Chess
variants.special: An 11×10 board. Camels replace bishops; Wildebeests (Knight+Camel compound) flank the queen.

variants.title: Absorption Chess
variants.special: Capturing piece permanently gains the victim's movement abilities. Absorptions stack.

variants.title: Almost Chess
variants.special: White's Queen is replaced by a Chancellor (Rook + Knight compound).

variants.title: Amazon Chess
variants.special: Queens replaced by Amazons (Queen + Knight). The most powerful piece possible.

variants.title: Andernach Chess
variants.special: Capturing piece changes colour (becomes opponent's). Kings exempt.

variants.title: Anti-King Chess II
variants.win: Checkmate the opponent's King or Anti-King
variants.special: Each player adds an Anti-King — a royal piece in check whenever it is NOT attacked by enemy pieces. Win by checkmating either the King or the Anti-King. Anti-Kings cannot capture enemy pieces.

variants.title: Antichess
variants.win: Lose all pieces or get stalemated
variants.special: Captures are mandatory. First to lose all pieces wins.

variants.title: Archchess
variants.special: 10×10 chess variant by Dr. Francesco Piacenza (Turin, 1683). Adds two new pieces per side: the Centurion (Dabbaba + Alfil + Knight compound; can jump) and the Decurion (one square diagonally). Pawns always promote to Queen. Unusual flexible castling rules including a King’s Leap option.

variants.title: ASEAN Chess
variants.special: Standardized Southeast Asian chess for regional competition. Makruk-family rules: Bishop moves 1 step diagonally, Pawns start on rank 2, promote on rank 6 to Ferz. Streamlined counting draw rules. Codified by ASEAN Chess Federation.

variants.title: Atomic Chess
variants.special: Captures cause explosions destroying all pieces on adjacent squares.

variants.title: Avalanche Chess
variants.special: Each turn has two parts: first make a legal chess move, then push one of the opponent's pawns one square forward. The push is obligatory. If pushing a pawn leaves your King in check, you lose immediately.

variants.title: Balbo's Chess
variants.board: Diamond-shaped, 70 squares (ranks 3-5-7-9-11-11-9-7-5-3, centred on file f)
variants.special: Chess on an unusual diamond-shaped board invented by M.G. Balbo (1974). Ten ranks of widths 3-5-7-9-11-11-9-7-5-3, all centred on file f, giving 70 squares across files a-k. Promotion rules are location-dependent: corner promotion squares allow minor pieces only. Pritchard warns that both sides have a third-move mate available from the starting position.

variants.title: Benedict Chess
variants.special: No captures. Attacked enemies convert to your colour instead.

variants.title: Berolina Chess
variants.special: Pawns move diagonally forward and capture straight forward — the inverse of normal.

variants.title: Berserk Chess
variants.special: Delivering check grants one bonus move with a different piece.

variants.title: Bird's Chess
variants.special: 1874 variant on a 10×8 board. Adds Guard (Rook+Knight) and Equerry (Bishop+Knight). A predecessor to Capablanca’s Chess. Castling: King moves three squares, Rook jumps over to the adjacent square.

variants.title: Blind Chess (Banqi)
variants.win: Capture all opponent's face-up pieces (opponent with no legal moves loses)
variants.special: Chinese hidden-piece game (Banqi, 暗棋) played on a 4×8 board (half a Xiangqi board). All 32 pieces placed face-down randomly. Each turn: flip a piece, move a piece, or capture. Piece ranks are unknown until revealed. Capture hierarchy: General defeats all except Soldier; Soldier defeats General. Cannon captures by jumping over exactly one screen (Taiwanese rules).

variants.title: Breakthrough
variants.special: Pawns only — first to reach the far side wins. No captures backward.

variants.title: Brusky's Hexagonal Chess
variants.special: Horizontal 84-hex board. 10 pawns per side. Unmoved pawns may also capture straight forward. Blockage rule applies. Invented Yakov Brusky.

variants.title: Byzantine Chess
variants.win: Checkmate, stalemate the opponent, or bare the opponent's King
variants.special: Played on a circular board of 4 concentric rings and 16 files (64 squares). Uses Shatranj piece movements: Bishops leap two diagonal squares, Queens move one diagonal square. Stalemate is a win. Baring the opponent's King wins unless the opponent can bare back immediately.

variants.title: Capablanca Chess
variants.special: Two extra pieces: Archbishop (B+N) and Chancellor (R+N). Wider board.

variants.title: Carrera's Chess
variants.special: 1617 historical variant on a 10×8 board. Adds Champion (Rook+Knight) and Centaur (Bishop+Knight). No castling, no en passant. A pawn double move is forbidden if it would both block a check and pass through an enemy pawn’s capture square.

variants.title: Centennial Chess
variants.special: 10×10 chess variant with four new pieces: the Steward (quadra-pawn, moves as pawn in all 4 directions), the Camel (2+1 oblique leap, colorbound), the Murray Lion (leaps to 2nd square orthogonally/diagonally or captures as King), and the Rotating Spearman (slides forward/backward and rotates between 3 orientations). Two moves per turn until first capture. En passant disabled. Created by John William Brown, 1999. Entry in the 1999 Large Variant Contest.

variants.title: Chak
variants.special: Mesoamerican-themed chess on a 9×9 board. Win by mating the Ajaw or landing your promoted Ajaw on the opponent's temple square. Pieces promote when crossing the river. Designed by Corey Clark, 2020.

variants.title: Chancellor Chess
variants.special: 9×9 chess variant published by Ben Foster (1889). Adds one Chancellor (Rook+Knight compound) per side, placed to the right of the King. Black squares are in the corners. Castling: King moves 2 squares, Rook moves 3. Pawns may promote to Chancellor.

variants.title: Chaturanga
variants.special: Ancient Indian ancestor of all chess variants, c. 600 CE. Weak counsellor and leaping elephant.

variants.title: Checkless Chess
variants.special: Cannot give check unless it is checkmate. King becomes aggressive.

variants.title: Chennis
variants.special: Tennis-themed chess on a 7×7 board. Win by advancing a Pawn to the opponent's back rank. A net across rank 4 prevents most pieces from crossing. Knights may jump the net freely. Designed by Corey Clark.

variants.title: Chigorin
variants.special: White's Bishops replaced by Knights. Four Knights vs standard army.

variants.title: Circular Chess
variants.special: Played on a circular board of 64 squares arranged in 4 concentric rings of 16 files. No castling, no en passant. Pawns promote after travelling 6 squares. Null moves (moving a piece all the way around a ring back to its start) are illegal.

variants.title: Citadel Chess
variants.win: Checkmate or stalemate; reaching the opponent's citadel is a draw
variants.special: Historical Shatranj variant (Shatranj al-Husun, 'Chess of the Fortresses'). 10×10 board plus four corner citadel squares. A King entering the opponent's citadel and surviving one move achieves a draw. Stalemate is a win. War Machines move as Bishops. No bare King rule.

variants.title: Codrus
variants.special: No check exists. You win by getting your own King captured.

variants.title: Congo
variants.special: 7×7 chess variant by Demian Freeling (1982, age 7). Six unique piece types: Lion (King, confined to castle), Zebra (Knight), Giraffe (2-step jump + king move), Elephant (1–2 step ortho leaper), Crocodile (king move + rook toward/in river), Monkey (capturing draughts-leaper). River rank in the centre. Drowning rule: non-Crocodile pieces left in the river for a full turn are removed. No check or checkmate — capture the Lion to win.

variants.title: Courier Chess
variants.special: Medieval German variant from 1202. Courier (modern bishop), Mann, Schleich (orthogonal-only), and Alfil on a 12-wide board.

variants.title: Crazy 38's
variants.win: Checkmate the opponent's King OR move your King to the opponent's Home Square
variants.special: 38-square chess variant by Ben Good, entered in the 1998 38 Squares Contest. Uses Shogi-style drops. Unique piece set: King, Rook, Bishop, Knight, Silver General, Gold General, and 4 Pawns per side — with movements distinct from standard Shogi. The board has a built-in loop connection that Rooks can exploit. Pawns promote to Queen only on the opponent's Home Square; captured Queens revert to Pawns before being dropped. Dual win condition: checkmate OR King reaches opponent's Home Square.

variants.title: Crazyhouse
variants.special: Captured pieces switch sides and can be dropped back onto the board.

variants.title: Cylinder Chess
variants.special: Files wrap — the a-file connects to the h-file. Pieces slide around the cylinder.

variants.title: Cylindrical Chess
variants.special: The board is treated as a cylinder: file a connects directly to file h. Pieces can move and attack across the edge. Bishops and queens are significantly stronger than in standard chess.

variants.title: Dark Chess
variants.special: Total fog — only see squares occupied by your own pieces.

variants.title: De Vasa's Hexagonal Chess
variants.special: Horizontally-oriented rhombus board of 81 hexes. Pawns start on rank 3. Castling permitted. Invented Helge E. de Vasa.

variants.title: Delirious Bughouse
variants.win: Capture an opposing King (team loses if either ally's King is captured)
variants.special: Bughouse variant by Alberto Monteiro (c.1984) combining relay capture, dice, and a worst-move mechanic. Two boards, 4 players, 2 allied teams. Key Bughouse modifications: Pawns drop only on ranks 2–6 (not rank 7); promoted Pawns when captured stay promoted (the promoting player recovers the original Pawn, permanently increasing piece count). Add-on layers: Dice Chess (die each turn — 1=Pawn, 2=Knight, 3=Bishop, 4=Rook, 5=Queen, 6=any); Worst Move (second die determines whether the player or opponent chooses the move); fairy pieces (Camel, Giraffe, Zebra, Cylindrical pieces, Pyramid, Atomic Bomb). Final full form adds Structures, Events, and Magic Items.

variants.title: Diana Chess
variants.special: 6×6 board. No queens or knights — bishops and rooks only.

variants.title: Dice Chess
variants.special: Die roll constrains which piece type must move.

variants.title: Displacement Chess
variants.special: Pieces can swap positions with adjacent friendly pieces as an alternative move.

variants.title: Djambi
variants.win: Be the last player with a Chief remaining
variants.special: 4-player political strategy on a 9×9 grid. Killed pieces remain as impassable corpses; the center Maze grants extra turns and immunities.

variants.title: Dragon Chess
variants.special: Created by Grandmaster Miguel Illescas. Standard chess with two Dragons (Bishop+Knight = Archbishop) held in reserve; at any point instead of a move, gate one onto any empty square on your own first rank.

variants.title: Duck Chess
variants.special: After each move, place the duck (blocker) on any empty square.

variants.title: Einstein Chess
variants.special: Non-capturing moves demote pieces; captures promote them (Q→R→B→N→P / P→N→B→R→Q).

variants.title: Empire Chess
variants.special: Asymmetric: FIDE Kingdom vs. Empire dynasty. Empire pieces move like Queens but capture in limited piece-specific ways. Faceoff rule: open-file confrontation between royal pieces loses for the creator. Designed by Couch Tomato, 2020.

variants.title: Endgame Chess
variants.special: Only Kings and pawns. Pure endgame technique from move one.

variants.title: Extinction Chess
variants.win: Capture all of one piece type
variants.special: Lose all your knights, bishops, rooks, or pawns — you lose the game.

variants.title: Fanorona Chess
variants.special: Chess variant on the double Alquerque board used in Fanorona (the traditional Malagasy game of Madagascar). Captures are by approach and withdrawal, not replacement: moving toward an enemy piece captures it; moving away from an enemy piece also captures it. If a capture is available, it must be made. Stalemate is a loss. No castling; no en passant; Pawn promotes only to previously captured pieces. Created by Peter Aronson, 2004.

variants.title: Fischer Random (Chess960)
variants.special: Back rank pieces randomised (960 positions). Castling rules adapted.

variants.title: Five-Check
variants.special: Extended Three-Check — five checks wins instead of three.

variants.title: Flip Chess
variants.special: Chess variant on a 38-square board with an unusual shape. 'Bare king loses' — a player whose King is the only piece remaining loses immediately, regardless of whether they are in check. No initial double Pawn moves. Companion to Crazy 38's (both are 38-square chess variants by John William Brown). Acclaimed 38-square variant; Java applet implementation by Ed Friedlander on chessvariants.com. Created 1999.

variants.title: Fog of War Chess
variants.special: You only see squares your pieces can move to. No check warnings.

variants.title: Four-Handed Chess (Chaturaji)
variants.win: Accumulate the most points from captures; 54 points for capturing all three enemy Kings
variants.special: Ancient Indian 4-player dice chess (c. 1030 CE). No checkmate — Kings are captured for points. Dice determine which piece type moves.

variants.title: Giveaway
variants.special: Forced captures. King is not royal. Stalemate is a loss.

variants.title: Glinski's Hexagonal Chess
variants.special: Chess on a 91-cell hexagonal board. Pieces slide along hex edges and vertices. Three bishops per side (one per cell colour).

variants.title: Grand Chess
variants.special: Same new pieces as Capablanca, bigger board, pawns start on rank 3.

variants.title: Grande Acedrex
variants.win: Checkmate, bare the King, or stalemate
variants.special: Large medieval Spanish chess variant from the Libro de los Juegos (Alfonso X, c. 1283). 12×12 board with six unique piece types: Griffion, Unicorn, Lion, Giraffe, Crocodile, and Rook. Pawns start on rank 4; ranks 2–3 are empty. Unique promotion rule: pawn promotes to the piece type that started on that file.

variants.title: Grid Chess
variants.special: Moves must cross at least one 2×2 grid line.

variants.title: Gustav III's Chess
variants.special: Swedish historical chess variant also known as Shakspel. Standard 8×8 chess with four extra squares added at the corners, each occupied by an Amazon (a piece combining Queen and Knight moves). Each side has 2 Amazons in addition to the standard FIDE army. Created by Gustav Johan Billberg, 1839. Jocly implementation available on chessvariants.com.

variants.title: Half Chess
variants.special: 4-rank board, armies start adjacent. Immediate contact.

variants.title: Hexapawn
variants.win: Advance a Pawn to the last rank, OR leave opponent with no legal moves
variants.special: 3×3 pawn-only game invented by Martin Gardner (Scientific American, March 1962) as a teaching tool for minimax strategy and machine learning. Six pawns total (3 per side). Solved game: Black wins with perfect play. No double-step; reaching the far rank wins immediately.

variants.title: Hole Chess
variants.win: Capture or checkmate the opponent's King
variants.special: 44-square chess variant on a custom board with two permanent holes — squares pieces cannot occupy, but through which pieces can be 'sucked.' The Queen, Rook, and PS-Bishop (Dragon Horse) each have a Two-Action Rule: they may move normally AND pull an enemy piece in their line of fire into a hole on the same turn. Named for the 44-square contest. Gary K. Gifford, 2003.

variants.title: Hoppel-Poppel
variants.special: Knights capture like bishops (sliding diagonal); bishops capture like knights (L-jump).

variants.title: Horde Chess
variants.win: White checkmates or Black destroys horde
variants.special: White has a full army. Black has 36 pawns. Asymmetric survival.

variants.title: Hostage Chess
variants.special: Shogi-inspired drop variant using a single standard set. Captured pieces become "hostages"; you can rescue yours by releasing one of theirs. Promoted pawns are replaced by prison pieces. Named chess variant of the decade by David Pritchard (Variant Chess, Summer 1999).

variants.title: Immunization Chess
variants.special: When a capture occurs, adjacent enemy pieces become immune to capture for 2 turns.

variants.title: Janus Chess
variants.special: Played on a 10×8 board. Each player adds two Januses (Archbishop: Bishop + Knight combined) between the Rooks and Knights. Castling sends the King to the b-file (3 squares) or i-file (4 squares).

variants.title: Khan's Chess
variants.special: Asymmetric: White plays FIDE chess, Gold commands the Mongol Horde — all Horde pieces except Khan and Kheshig are divergent (move ≠ capture). Stalemate is a loss. Campmate wins (King to opponent's back rank).

variants.title: King of the Hill
variants.win: Checkmate or king reaches centre 4 squares
variants.special: Moving your king to d4/d5/e4/e5 is an instant win.

variants.title: Klein Bottle Chess
variants.special: Chess on a Klein bottle: an 8x14 board (double-height Cylindrical Chess) where files a and h are joined (as in Cylindrical Chess), AND the rank-11/12 seam is joined with a half-twist that mirrors file position. Each side has 16 pawns across two ranks. Kings face the opponent's Queen, not the opponent's King. Bishops are not colour-bound but can reach only 3/8 of the board in one move. Invented by Alberto Monteiro.

variants.title: Knightmate
variants.special: Knight and King swap roles. The Knight is royal; Kings move as knights.

variants.title: Kriegspiel
variants.special: Fog-of-war chess. Each player sees only their own pieces. A referee manages a master board and announces partial information: legality of attempted moves, check direction, capture location, and pawn-capture availability.

variants.title: Legan Chess
variants.special: Berolina pawns (move diagonal, capture straight). King and Queen swap starting squares.

variants.title: Los Alamos Vierschach
variants.special: 4-player chess by Jörg Knappen combining Los Alamos Chess (6×6, no Bishops, no castling) with the Vierschach 4-player format. Non-competing entry to the 84 Squares Contest. Board: a 6×6 grid extended by 2×6 squares on each of the four sides, identical to the Quintessential Chess board (84 squares total). Four Los Alamos armies arranged as in Vierschach with allied teams side by side. Pawns gain initial double-step since the promotion path is longer than in standard Los Alamos; en passant applies. No castling.

variants.title: Los Alamos
variants.special: First computer chess (1956). 6x6 board, no Bishops, no castling.

variants.title: Madrasi Chess
variants.special: Same-type opposing pieces paralyse each other when they attack.

variants.title: Maharaja & Sepoys
variants.special: One player has a full army. The other has one piece that moves as queen + knight.

variants.title: Makpong
variants.special: King cannot move out of check. You must block or capture instead.

variants.title: Makruk
variants.special: Thai chess. Khon moves 5 directions (silver general). Pawns promote on rank 6 to Met. No castling or en passant.

variants.title: Mansindam (Pantheon Tale)
variants.special: 9×9 board with Shogi-style drops and mandatory promotion in the enemy camp. Compound pieces: Cardinal (B+N), Marshal (R+N), Angel (Q+N). Campmate wins. Stalemate is a loss; no draws possible.

variants.title: Marseillais Chess
variants.special: Each player makes TWO moves per turn (except White's first turn).

variants.title: McCooey's Hexagonal Chess
variants.special: Same 91-hex board as Gliński, but diagonal pawn captures, 7 pawns per side, and stalemate is a draw. Invented Dave McCooey.

variants.title: Medusa Chess
variants.special: After the queen moves, all enemy pieces she attacks become petrified for 2 turns.

variants.title: Metamachy
variants.special: 12×12 board with 12 piece types. Variable starting position: King, Queen, Lion, Eagle may be placed in any arrangement on their four squares; Black decides, White mirrors. Cannon slides/Xiangqi-captures; Camel leaps (1,3); Eagle bends diagonal then slides orthogonal; Lion leaps anywhere within 2 King steps.

variants.title: Mini Hexchess
variants.special: 37-hex board, 7 files, no Queen piece. All 7 opponent-side hexes are promotion squares. Promotes to R/B/N only. Invented Dave McCooey, 1997.

variants.title: Minichess
variants.special: Gardner's 5x5 board. All piece types, fast tactical games.

variants.title: Möbius Strip Chess
variants.special: Chess on a Möbius strip: an 8x14 board (double-height Cylindrical Chess) where files a and h wrap normally, and the rank-11/12 seam joins with a half-twist that mirrors file position. Each side has 16 pawns across two ranks, advancing from both ends of the strip toward the middle and toward the twisted seam. Kings face the opponent's Queen, not the opponent's King. Bishops are not colour-bound. Invented by Alberto Monteiro.

variants.title: Monster Chess
variants.special: White moves twice per turn but starts with only King, Rooks, and pawns.

variants.title: No Castling Chess
variants.special: Standard chess with castling removed. Kings must develop naturally.

variants.title: No Retreat
variants.special: Pieces cannot move backward toward their own starting rank.

variants.title: Oblong Chess
variants.special: Historical chess variant on a 4×16 board (four files, sixteen ranks). Approximately one thousand years old. A variant of Shatranj — the Arabic predecessor of modern chess — using the full Shatranj piece set. Seven different starting setups are documented. Often played with dice that determine which piece type may move each turn. The extreme rectangular board shifts piece values significantly: Rooks are very strong on the long 16-rank axis.

variants.title: Omega Chess
variants.special: Commercial variant on a 10×10 board with 4 extra "wizard squares" beyond the corners (104 total squares). Adds Champion (WAD: leaps 2 ortho/diag or slides 1 ortho) and Wizard (FC: leaps (1,3)/(3,1) or slides 1 diag). Pawns may advance 1, 2, or 3 squares on first move.

variants.title: Omnicide
variants.special: Lose all your pieces to win. Captures NOT forced (unlike Antichess).

variants.title: Orda Chess
variants.special: Asymmetric: White plays standard. Black commands the Horde — divergent movers that move one way and capture another.

variants.title: Orda Mirror
variants.special: Both players command the Horde army from Orda Chess. Every piece moves as a Knight but captures as its FIDE counterpart. Designed by Corey Clark, 2020.

variants.title: Ouk Chaktrang (Cambodian Chess)
variants.special: Cambodian chess. Koul leaps 1 or 2 squares diagonally; King may jump as a Knight on its first move. Pawns promote on rank 6. Codified by the Asian Chess Federation.

variants.title: Patrol Chess
variants.special: Pieces can only capture or give check when defended by a friendly piece.

variants.title: Pawns Only
variants.special: Kings and pawns only. First to promote wins instantly.

variants.title: Peasants' Revolt
variants.special: White has King + 8 pawns vs Black's King + 2 Knights + 8 pawns.

variants.title: Petty Chess
variants.special: All piece types on a compact 5×6 board. Single copies of each.

variants.title: Placement Chess
variants.special: Players take turns placing their back-rank pieces before the game begins. Bishops must be on opposite-colored squares. Designed by David Bronstein; also published as a Chess Variant Pages format.

variants.title: Pocket Knight Chess
variants.special: Each player holds one extra Knight in reserve (the "pocket"). Once per game, instead of making a normal move, a player may drop their pocket Knight onto any empty square.

variants.title: Poison Chess
variants.special: Capture squares become poisoned for 3 turns — non-king pieces landing there are destroyed.

variants.title: Progressive
variants.special: Moves per turn escalate: 1, 2, 3, 4... Check ends your turn early.

variants.title: Racing Kings
variants.special: No checks allowed. Both kings start on 1st rank. Race to the top.

variants.title: Raumschach
variants.special: Three-dimensional chess on five stacked 5×5 boards. Adds the Unicorn (triagonal slider). Pawns move forward or upward; capture diagonally. No castling, no en passant, no double push.

variants.title: Recruitment Chess
variants.special: Captured pieces defect to the captor and appear on the vacated square.

variants.title: Rifle Chess
variants.special: Capturing pieces stay on their square — they 'shoot' the target.

variants.title: Rollerball
variants.win: Checkmate the King, OR King clockwise-reaches opponent's King starting square
variants.special: Chess variant on a 40-square ring board (7×7 grid with 3×3 centre removed). Two concentric rings: outer (24 squares) and inner (16 squares). Each side has only 6 pieces: King, Bishop, 2 Rooks, 2 Pawns. Pieces move clockwise-dominant (most cannot slide backward). Jean-Louis Cazaux, 1999, 40-squares contest.

variants.title: Romanchenko's Chess
variants.special: Standard FIDE chess pieces and rules on a board with 'broken columns' — certain file columns are displaced or interrupted at specific ranks, breaking the standard 8×8 grid alignment and preventing rote pattern memorization. Designed by Soviet chess trainer V. Romanchenko as a pedagogical tool: players must reason from first principles rather than imitate memorized openings. Jocly implementation on chessvariants.com.

variants.title: S-Chess (Seirawan Chess)
variants.special: Two new compound pieces — Hawk and Elephant — enter the board via a gating mechanic when back-rank pieces leave their starting squares. Designed by Yasser Seirawan and Jonathan Tisdall, 2007.

variants.title: Senterej
variants.special: Ethiopian Shatranj variant with a unique mobilization phase: before the first capture, both players move simultaneously without turns. Shatranj-style pieces (Fil leaps diagonally 2, Ferz moves 1 diagonal). No castling, no en passant.

variants.title: Shafran's Hexagonal Chess
variants.special: Smaller 70-hex board with 9 files. Castling permitted. Variable pawn initial step by file. Invented Boris Shafran.

variants.title: Shako
variants.special: 10×10 board adding the Cannon (slides to move, leaps over a platform to capture) and Elephant (leaps 2 diagonally). Designed by Jean-Louis Cazaux, 2000.

variants.title: Shatar
variants.special: Mongolian chess. Check exists (shak/dug/tsod). Mate must include a shak. Knight cannot deliver mate. Bare king is a draw. Obligatory opening 1.d4 d5.

variants.title: Shatranj Kamil
variants.special: ‘Complete Chess’ — a historical Arabic chess variant (~1000 years old) on a 10×10 board. Adds two War Machines (Dabbabah) per side to the standard Shatranj set. War Machines move as Kings but are immune to check. Unique promotion rule: a Pawn can only promote when the player has no General on the board.

variants.title: Shatranj
variants.special: Medieval Islamic chess. Bare king and stalemate are both wins. Ancestor of modern chess.

variants.title: Shinobi Chess
variants.special: Asymmetric: FIDE Kingdom vs. Shinobi Clan. Shinobi starts with fewer pieces but gains new pieces by dropping clan members held in hand. Shinobi pieces promote on reaching the promotion zone. Designed by Corey Clark, 2021.

variants.title: Shinobi+
variants.win: Checkmate or campmate (King/Kage reaches opponent's last rank)
variants.special: Rebalanced Shinobi Chess. The Clan (Pink) moves first, starts with most pieces in hand including a new Fox piece (Bishop+King hybrid). Kingdom Pawns promote on rank 6. Perpetual check is a loss. Designed by Couch Tomato, 2021.

variants.title: Shogun Chess
variants.special: Zone-triggered automatic promotion and Shogi-style drops from captured pieces. Designed by Corey Clark, 2020.

variants.title: Single-Check
variants.special: One check wins. No checkmate needed — any single check ends the game.

variants.title: Sittuyin
variants.special: Burmese chess. Placement opening phase. Pawns promote on the diagonal. No castling or en passant.

variants.title: Spartan Chess
variants.special: Asymmetric: Persian (standard FIDE) vs. Spartan army with two Kings and unique pieces. Designed by Steven Streetman, 2010.

variants.title: Spherical Chess
variants.special: Chess on a sphere — a surface with no edges and no corners, where ranks and files meet at poles. The standard 8×8 board is played with two wrapping rules: ranks wrap horizontally (left-right, as in Cylindrical Chess), and files meet at polar singularities where a piece crossing the pole continues four files away. Multiple documented versions from 1950–2014; this file documents the family and the most widely agreed rules. Bishops are colourbound. Knights have 8 possible moves from any position.

variants.title: Stalemate Wins
variants.special: Standard chess but stalemate is a win, not a draw.

variants.title: Stupidhouse
variants.special: Bughouse chess variant where received pieces are placed on a randomly selected empty square rather than a player-chosen square. When a player captures a piece, it passes to their partner — but when the partner uses it, it lands on a random legal empty square instead of a chosen one. Removes strategic drop placement and replaces it with chaos.

variants.title: Suicide Chess
variants.special: Forced captures like Giveaway, but stalemate is a draw, not a loss.

variants.title: Synochess
variants.special: Asymmetric: Western (FIDE) vs. Eastern dynasty (Xiangqi-derived pieces, Cannon, Chariot, Soldier drops). Faceoff rule ends the game if royal pieces face each other unobstructed. Designed by Corey Clark, 2020.

variants.title: Tamerlane Chess
variants.win: Checkmate (or bare king with citadel draw)
variants.special: Medieval 14th-century chess of Timur. 28 pieces per side, 12 piece types, three-stage promoting pawn, citadel draw rule.

variants.title: Tandem Chess
variants.win: Checkmate either opposing King across both boards
variants.special: Team chess variant for 2×2 players on two simultaneous boards. Captured pieces are passed to the partner for dropping on the partner's board. Also known as Siamese Chess. Key differences from Bughouse: (1) no check or checkmate by drop; (2) match continues until both games complete. Invented ~1960s.

variants.title: Teleportation Chess
variants.special: Each side has 3 teleports per game — move any piece to any empty square.

variants.title: Three-Check
variants.special: First to check the opponent three times wins.

variants.title: Toroidal Byzantine Chess
variants.board: 4-ring torus (4×16 circular board with radial wrap)
variants.special: Byzantine Chess (historical Shatranj on a 4×16 circular board) combined with toroidal topology: the innermost ring connects to the outermost ring radially, in addition to the standard circular wrap along each ring. A piece sliding inward past ring 4 emerges from ring 1; a piece sliding outward past ring 1 emerges from ring 4. Invented by Anatoly Khalfine and Ernst Saperow, circa 1999–2001.

variants.title: Gadsden's Toroidal Chess
variants.special: Chess on a torus — all four edges wrap. Moving off the right edge (h-file) reappears on the left (a-file); moving off rank 8 reappears on rank 1. Every square has exactly 8 neighbours; there are no edge squares and no corner squares. Uses a three-rank starting position per side with an extra set of pawns (32 pawns total). Invented around 1990 by Richard Gadsden and Phil Roberts as a variant of Cylindrical Chess.

variants.title: Torpedo Chess
variants.special: Pawns can move two squares forward from any rank, not just the starting rank.

variants.title: Turkish Great Chess II (Atranj)
variants.special: Historical large chess variant known as Atranj or Qatranj, described by H. J. R. Murray in A History of Chess. Played on a 10×10 board with an expanded piece set including the Prince (moves as Rook, Bishop, or Knight), Kotwal (Bishop or Knight), and Urdabegini (moves one square toward the opposing King). Despite its Turkish classification in Murray's work, the source manuscript is Indian. No castling.

variants.title: Turkish Great Chess III
variants.special: Historical large chess variant played on a 12×12 board. One of four Ottoman/Indian large chess variants catalogued by John Gollon from H. J. R. Murray's A History of Chess. Expands the standard chess piece set with multiple piece types that move as Bishop (Fil, Dahja) and adds the Chariot (Ratha, moves as Rook) alongside two Rooks. The Wazir moves as a full Queen. No castling; no Pawn double step.

variants.title: Turkish Great Chess IV
variants.special: Historical large chess variant played on a 14×14 board. Despite its Turkish classification, it includes Indian and Persian piece names (Raja, Rani, Shahzadeh) suggesting a mixed cultural origin. The Rani (Queen) is weak — moving only one square in any direction — and uniquely may be placed or left en prise without penalty. No castling; no Pawn double step.

variants.title: Ultima (Baroque Chess)
variants.special: All seven piece types use entirely different capture mechanics. No check: win by physically capturing the opponent's King. Designed by Robert Abbott, 1962.

variants.title: Upside-Down
variants.special: Pieces start on the opponent's back rank. Instant tactical chaos.

variants.title: Vierschach
variants.win: Checkmate the last surviving enemy King
variants.special: Traditional German 4-player chess invented by Dr. G. Arthur Lutze (1813–1870). Cross-shaped 160-square board. Two teams of two, allied armies placed side by side. Standard FIDE movement. First enemy King may be captured normally; second enemy King must be checkmated.

variants.title: Weak!
variants.special: Weakest piece type with a legal move must move first.

variants.title: Xiang Fu
variants.win: Duple Checkmate, or capture one Champion then checkmate the remaining one
variants.special: Xiangqi/chess hybrid by Eventlesstew for the PyChess Variant Design Contest. 9×9 board, dual Champions (royal), Crossbow (diagonal Cannon), piece drops within first two ranks, captures go to hand.

variants.title: Yalta Chess
variants.win: Be the last player with a King remaining
variants.special: 3-player chess on a hexagonal board divided into three Y-shaped sectors, one per player (Red, Green, Blue), meeting at a central junction. Checkmating a player captures their army. Alliances encouraged.

games.title: Dou Shou Qi (斗兽棋 / Jungle)
games.tagline: Animals battle across rivers and traps to reach the enemy den
games.how_to_play: Move your 8 ranked animal pieces (Rat to Elephant) toward the opponent's Den. Higher rank captures lower, but the Rat defeats the Elephant. Traps weaken defenders, rivers block most pieces.

games.title: Double-Six Dominoes
games.tagline: Match the pips, build the chain, score the ends
games.how_to_play: The double-6 domino set (28 tiles) supports 4 games: Block, All Fives, Mexican Train, and Chickenfoot. All involve matching pip values and extending a chain.

games.title: Draughts
games.tagline: The world's oldest family of capture games
games.how_to_play: Move pieces diagonally and capture opponents by jumping over them. Men promote to kings with extended movement. Mandatory captures force tactical sacrifices.

variants.title: English Draughts
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: Diagonal movement only. No flying kings. Free choice between captures.

variants.title: Turkish Draughts
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: Orthogonal movement replaces diagonal. Majority capture rule. Immediate removal.

variants.title: International Draughts
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: Flying kings. Mandatory longest chain. Men capture backwards. Delayed removal.

variants.title: Frisian Draughts
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: Captures in all 8 directions. 3-move king limit. King preference on equal chains.

variants.title: Lasca
variants.win: Block or bury all opponent pieces
variants.special: Column stacking. Captured pieces go underneath the captor. All 22 pieces stay in play forever.

variants.title: Alquerque
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: The common ancestor. Movement along lines (orthogonal and diagonal). No promotion.

variants.title: Russian Draughts
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: Men capture backwards. Mid-jump promotion. No majority rule. Free choice between captures.

variants.title: Brazilian Draughts
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: International rules on 8×8 board. Flying kings. Majority capture. Delayed removal.

variants.title: Canadian Draughts
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: Largest standard board (12×12). 30 pieces per side. International rules. Longest games.

variants.title: Pool Checkers
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: Men capture both directions. Flying kings. Mid-jump promotion. Free choice. US federation since 1966.

variants.title: Italian Draughts
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: Men cannot capture kings. Strict capture priority: king captures first, then most pieces, then most kings.

variants.title: Spanish Draughts
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: Flying kings. Men cannot capture backwards. Majority rule with king preference.

variants.title: Czech Draughts
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: King captures take priority over man captures. Mid-jump promotion. No majority rule for men.

variants.title: Thai Draughts
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: Only 8 pieces per side. Flying kings must stop immediately behind captured piece. Forward-only men.

variants.title: Bashni
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent commanders
variants.special: Column stacking on 8×8. Russian movement rules. Captured pieces form towers. Predecessor to Lasca.

variants.title: Dameo
variants.special: Phalanx movement: lines of men slide together. Orthogonal captures only. 18 pieces per side.

variants.title: Diagonal Draughts
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: Pieces start along the diagonal. The long diagonal of the board is empty at setup.

variants.title: German Draughts
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: Men capture both forwards and backwards. Flying kings. No majority capture rule.

variants.title: Ghanaian Draughts
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: Men do not capture backwards. No majority rule. A player reduced to one piece loses.

variants.title: Spantsiretti
variants.win: Capture or block all opponent pieces
variants.special: Russian Draughts rules on a wider 10×8 board. 20 pieces per side.

games.title: Dungeon Chess
games.tagline: Asymmetric fantasy strategy on modular dungeon boards
games.how_to_play: Draft asymmetric armies from 4 factions (Human, Undead, Redskin, Greenskin) using an XP budget. Battle on modular dungeon maps with terrain hazards. King capture wins.

games.title: Dungeon World
games.tagline: Powered by the Apocalypse fantasy dungeon-crawling, fiction-first play
games.how_to_play: Narrate fiction first; when a character's action triggers a move, roll 2d6+stat. 10+ is full success, 7-9 is partial success, 6- is GM move. The GM never rolls dice.

games.title: Dungeons & Dragons 5th Edition SRD
games.tagline: The open core rules for the world's most popular roleplaying game
games.how_to_play: Choose a race and class, roll d20 + modifiers against difficulty targets, and adventure through dungeons and quests. One player is DM, others are player characters with levels 1-20.

games.title: Econopoly
games.tagline: Euro-style resource management meets Monopoly
games.how_to_play: Choose one action per turn: move, trade, or build. Collect resources from decks, combine them for victory points. Game ends when a player goes bankrupt or decks empty — most VP wins.

games.title: Fanorona
games.tagline: The national game of Madagascar: capture by approach and withdrawal
games.how_to_play: Move pieces along lines on a 9×5 grid. Capture by moving toward an enemy line (approach) or away from one (withdrawal), taking all pieces in the unbroken line.

games.title: Fate Core
games.tagline: A flexible, narrative-first tabletop RPG built on aspects, fate points, and the four actions
games.how_to_play: Roll 4 Fate dice plus skill against the ladder. Characters defined by aspects (story phrases). Invoke aspects for bonuses, accept compels for fate points. Four actions: overcome, create advantage, attack, defend.

games.title: Flower 48
games.tagline: Japanese flower cards: 12 monthly suits, 48 cards
games.how_to_play: The Hanafuda deck (48 cards, 12 monthly suits) supports 4 games: Koi-Koi, Hana-Awase, Go-Stop, and Oicho-Kabu. All involve matching and collecting cards by suit or type.

games.title: Go
games.tagline: Four thousand years of emergent complexity from one rule
games.how_to_play: Place stones on grid intersections to surround territory and capture opponent groups by filling their liberties. From one fundamental rule emerges extraordinary strategic depth.

variants.title: Standard Go (19×19)
variants.special: Full tournament game. 361 intersections. Komi 6.5. Area or territory scoring.

variants.title: 13×13 Go
variants.special: Intermediate board. 169 intersections. Komi 5.5. 30–60 minute games.

variants.title: 9×9 Go
variants.special: Quick games (15 min). 81 intersections. Komi 5.5. Purely tactical.

variants.title: Gomoku
variants.special: Black plays first. Stones are placed, never moved. No captures.

variants.title: Ninuki-Renju
variants.win: Five in an unbroken row (exactly five) or five pairs captured
variants.special: Japanese precursor to Pente. Custodial captures. Two win conditions. Active 1923-1940.

variants.title: One-Colour Go
variants.special: Both players use identical stones. Must remember which are yours. Extreme memory challenge.

variants.title: Phantom Go
variants.special: Fog of war. Players cannot see opponent stones. A referee mediates all moves.

variants.title: Capture Go
variants.special: First player to capture any stone wins. No territory scoring. The universal teaching variant.

variants.title: Rengo
variants.special: Team Go. Partners alternate turns. No consultation. 2v2 or 3v3.

variants.title: Renju
variants.win: Five in an unbroken row (exactly five for Black)
variants.special: Competitive Gomoku with forbidden moves for Black. Governed by the Renju International Federation.

variants.title: Stoical Go
variants.special: Cannot capture if opponent captured last turn. Forces restraint and patience.

variants.title: Sunjang Baduk
variants.special: Korean historical Go. 16 pre-placed stones. Prisoners ignored. No komi.

variants.title: Tibetan Go
variants.special: 17×17 board. 12 pre-placed stones. Delayed captures. Unique scoring system.

variants.title: Toroidal Go
variants.special: Edges wrap horizontally and vertically. No corners, no edges, no joseki.

games.title: Halma
games.tagline: Race your pieces across the board before your opponent
games.how_to_play: Move your pieces from one corner camp to the diagonally opposite corner on a 16×16 board. Step to adjacent squares or chain-hop over any adjacent piece without capturing.

variants.title: Standard 2-Player Halma
variants.win: Move all your pieces into the opponent's corner camp
variants.special: Pieces may step or chain-hop in any direction. No capture. Once in the opponent's camp, pieces cannot leave.

variants.title: Standard 4-Player Halma
variants.win: Move all your pieces into the diagonally opposite corner camp
variants.special: Four players with 13 pieces each. Optional 2v2 team play with diagonal partners.

games.title: Hex
games.tagline: Connect your two edges across a diamond of hexagons
games.how_to_play: Place stones on a rhombus-shaped hex board. First player to form a connected chain linking their two opposite edges wins. A draw is topologically impossible.

variants.title: Hex (11×11)
variants.special: Standard tournament size. 121 cells. First player advantage offset by swap rule.

variants.title: Hex (9×9)
variants.special: Compact board. 81 cells. Quick tactical games.

variants.title: Hex (13×13)
variants.special: Large board. 169 cells. Deep strategic play.

variants.title: Hex (14×14)
variants.special: 196 cells. Used in some tournament formats.

variants.title: Hex (19×19)
variants.special: Maximum standard size. 361 cells. Marathon-length games.

variants.title: Y
variants.special: Triangular board. Win by connecting all three sides with a single chain. Generalises Hex to 3-edge connection.

variants.title: Y (Large — 15)
variants.special: Large Y board. Deep strategic play.

variants.title: Y (Small — 9)
variants.special: Compact Y board. Quick games.

games.title: Hyper Imperium
games.tagline: 3D exploration and mercenary factions for Twilight Imperium
games.how_to_play: Five modifications for Twilight Imperium 4e: 3D movement across outer rings, flexible trading with promissory notes, shared secret objectives, two new factions, and blind voting via influence cards.

games.title: Ironsworn
games.tagline: A perilous quest through the Ironlands, guided by vows and oracle tables
games.how_to_play: Roll action dice against challenge dice to resolve moves. Characters are bound to sworn vows, face peril, and mark progress. Plays solo, cooperatively, or with a guide. Oracle tables generate narrative.

games.title: Knave
games.tagline: A classless OSR rules toolkit for running old-school fantasy adventures
games.how_to_play: Roll d20 + ability bonus against difficulty. Every PC is a Knave whose role comes from what they carry, not a class. Simple encumbrance, unified defense system, concrete spellcasting.

games.title: L'Attaque
games.tagline: Hidden-rank warfare — the original family that spawned Stratego
games.how_to_play: Hidden-information strategy where pieces have hidden ranks. Higher rank defeats lower when pieces meet. Win conditions vary by variant: capture the Flag, land on the Aerodrome, or get Flags to your Base.

variants.title: Aviation
variants.win: Land a Troop Carrier on the opponent's Aerodrome. Draw if both sides lose all Troop Carriers.
variants.special: Hidden-information aerial warfare game by H.P. Gibson & Sons. 42 pieces per player: 32 numbered flying units plus 10 unnumbered Auxiliaries (Searchlights, Observation Balloons, Anti-Aircraft Guns). The Searchlight + Gun ranging system is unique: Searchlights reveal hidden pieces and enable AAA Guns to engage at range. Troop Carriers move only diagonally; are driven back (not removed) when attacked by a piece of value 5 or higher; win by reaching the opponent's Aerodrome.

variants.title: Dover Patrol
variants.win: Get both Flags — your own and the opponent's — onto your own Base
variants.special: Naval CTF (Capture the Flag) game by H.P. Gibson & Sons. 40 pieces per player plus a separate Flag clip. The Flag starts on the Base inside the walled Harbour; seizing the enemy Flag and conveying it to your own Base wins. The Flying Boat uniquely crosses the Harbour Wall and moves 2 squares; Mine Layers are movable floating mines; Submarines sink all ships except Mine Layers and Motor Torpedo Boats.

variants.title: L'Attaque (Standard)
variants.win: Capture the opponent's Flag, or leave them with no movable pieces
variants.special: Hidden-information land warfare game by Hermance Edan (1909). 36 pieces per player on a 9×10 board with three 1×2 lake areas. Higher rank defeats lower; Mines defeat all except Sappers; Spy defeats Commander-in-chief when Spy attacks.

variants.title: Tri-Tactics
variants.win: Occupy the opponent's H.Q. with a Land Infantry piece, OR occupy the opponent's Lake (Naval Base) with a Ship
variants.special: Combined-arms hidden-rank game by H.P. Gibson & Sons. 56 pieces per player across three services: Land (Infantry + Artillery), Naval (Ships + Flying Boats + Submarine), and Air Force, plus 8 Searchlights. All three services operate on a single board with land, sea, river, lake, and H.Q. terrain. Pieces caught out of their element are immediately forfeit when attacked. The Searchlight may move any number of squares in a straight line to attack. Combat outcomes between all 18 piece types are resolved via a published Value Table.

games.title: Mahjong
games.tagline: A tile-matching game of skill, strategy, and fortune
games.how_to_play: The 136-tile Mahjong set supports 5 regional variants: Hong Kong, Riichi, Taiwanese, Zung Jung, and American Classic. All involve drawing and discarding tiles to complete winning hands of melds and a pair.

games.title: Mancala
games.tagline: The world's most-played family of count-and-capture games
games.how_to_play: Sow seeds or stones from one pit around the board, capturing when sowing lands in the right conditions. Each variant has different capture rules, board sizes, and end conditions.

variants.title: Kalah
variants.special: Landing in your own store grants a bonus turn. Opponent's store is skipped during sowing.

variants.title: Oware
variants.special: Grand slam rule prevents a player from clearing all opponent seeds in a single turn.

variants.title: Bao
variants.win: Reduce opponent to no seeds in their inner row, or leave them with no legal move
variants.special: Two-phase game: namua (seeding phase) then mtaji (capture phase). Multi-lap relay sowing.

variants.title: Congkak
variants.win: Have more seeds in your house than the opponent at game end
variants.special: Sow into your own house but skip the opponent's house. Dead pits must be bought back.

variants.title: Toguz Korgool
variants.special: The tuzduk rule: landing the 3rd seed in an opponent's odd-numbered pit locks it as your permanent scoring pit.

variants.title: Pallanguzhi
variants.win: Capture all 168 seeds (opponent cannot fill pits to play)
variants.special: Multi-lap sowing: the last seed always triggers pickup of the next pit, creating long relay chains.

variants.title: Ayo
variants.special: Functionally identical to Oware; grand slam rule applies. Culturally distinct Yoruba tradition.

variants.title: Sungka
variants.win: Have more seeds in your head at game end
variants.special: Simultaneous start; sow only into your own head, never the opponent's.

games.title: Maze Rats
games.tagline: A minimalist toolkit for old-school-style sandbox adventuring
games.how_to_play: Roll dice and consult procedural tables to generate characters, spells, monsters, NPCs, treasure, cities, wilderness, and dungeons on the fly. One Game Master guides players through sandbox adventures using a single compact page of rules.

games.title: Nine Men's Morris
games.tagline: The ancient mill game, played on stone, cloth, and wood across five continents
games.how_to_play: Form three-in-a-row lines (mills) to capture opponent pieces. Place all pieces during the opening phase, then move them to form mills. Reduce your opponent to two pieces or block all their moves to win.

variants.title: Three Men's Morris
variants.win: Form a three-in-a-row with all three of your pieces
variants.special: No movement phase; pieces jump to any empty square. Smallest member of the Mill family.

variants.title: Six Men's Morris
variants.win: Reduce opponent to 2 pieces or block all their moves
variants.special: Two concentric squares with connecting lines. The medieval European standard form before Nine Men's Morris predominated.

variants.title: Nine Men's Morris
variants.win: Reduce opponent to 2 pieces or block all their moves
variants.special: Three concentric squares joined at midpoints. Flying allowed when reduced to 3 pieces.

variants.title: Twelve Men's Morris
variants.board: Three concentric squares with diagonals (24 intersections)
variants.win: Reduce opponent to 2 pieces or block all their moves
variants.special: Identical board to Nine Men's Morris but with corner diagonal connections. 12 pieces per side. No flying rule.

variants.title: Lasker Morris
variants.win: Reduce opponent to 2 pieces or block all their moves
variants.special: Each turn: either place a new piece OR move an existing piece. No sequential placement phase.

variants.title: Morabaraba
variants.win: Reduce opponent to 2 cows or block all their moves
variants.special: South African national game. Cows instead of men. Special rules for the three-cow endgame.

variants.title: Shax
variants.win: Reduce opponent to 2 pieces or block all their moves
variants.special: Somali variant: during placement, mills do not remove opponent pieces — instead, pieces are captured only during the movement phase.

games.title: Nukes: Official Rulebook
games.tagline: Cold-war territory control on a hex map with nuclear brinkmanship
games.how_to_play: Command armies across hex terrain, managing platoons that change type based on unit count. Return hostages to earn moves, but every return strengthens your opponent. Build bases to convert units into isotopes for nuclear strikes. Win by destroying or occupying an opponent's city.

variants.title: Nukes: Siege
variants.special: Hostage mechanic replaced with own-supply recruiting. Enemy hostages only arrive through combat.

variants.title: Nukes: Standard
variants.special: Standard 3-ring hex map with seeded terrain generation. 2-player default.

variants.title: Nukes: Asymmetric Powers
variants.special: Each player draws one Power Card at setup. No two players hold the same card.

variants.title: Nukes: Fallout
variants.special: Biohazard tiles spread one tile per round. City tiles are immune. The board shrinks over time.

games.title: Nyout (유놓이 / Yut Nori)
games.tagline: Korean stick-throwing race across a circular track
games.how_to_play: Throw four sticks to generate movement values. Race tokens around a circular track with shortcut branches. Capture opponent tokens to send them back to start. Stack tokens for combined movement but risk losing multiple at once. First team to move all tokens home wins.

games.title: Pachisi
games.tagline: The ancient Indian race game behind Ludo, Sorry!, and Trouble
games.how_to_play: Race four pieces around a cross-shaped board from your home to the opposite side. Throw cowrie shells for movement, land on castle squares for safety, and capture opponent pieces to send them home. Direct ancestor of Ludo, Sorry!, and Trouble.

variants.title: Pachisi (Standard)
variants.win: Move all four pieces from the Charkoni, around the board, and back home first
variants.special: Cowrie shell randomisation. Grace rolls on 0, 1, or 6 mouths up.

variants.title: 2-Player Pachisi
variants.win: Move all eight pieces (two colours) home before your opponent
variants.special: Each player controls two opposite arms. Rules otherwise identical to standard.

variants.title: Seven-Shell Pachisi
variants.win: Move all pieces home before your opponents
variants.special: Uses seven cowrie shells with named throw values. Higher potential scores than the standard six-shell form.

games.title: Pathfinder 1st Edition (PFSRD)
games.tagline: Paizo's fork of D&D 3.5, the most complete open ruleset in existence
games.how_to_play: Create characters from 11 classes and 7 races. Roll d20 + modifiers for skill checks, attacks, and saves. Build characters through feats, spells, and equipment. The most complete open ruleset in existence, evolved from D&D 3.5.

pages.title: Metamagic, Critical, and Item Creation Feats

games.title: Reversi
games.tagline: Flip your opponent's discs to claim the board
games.how_to_play: Place discs to flank and flip opponent pieces. Valid moves must flip at least one enemy disc by trapping it between your new disc and an existing one. The player with the most discs when no legal moves remain wins.

variants.title: Standard Reversi
variants.win: Most discs on the board when no moves remain
variants.special: The original 8×8 game as played in international competition since 1977.

variants.title: Six-by-Six Reversi
variants.win: Most discs on the board when no moves remain
variants.special: Smaller board for shorter games or competitive solving. Identical rules to standard Reversi.

variants.title: Anti-Reversi
variants.win: Fewest discs on the board when no moves remain
variants.special: Misère variant. Win condition inverted — giving up discs is the goal. Draw is possible.

games.title: Royal Game of Ur
games.tagline: The oldest known board game: reconstructed from 4,500-year-old clay tablets
games.how_to_play: Roll four tetrahedral dice to move pieces along an L-shaped track. Rosette squares grant extra rolls and safety from capture. Landing on opponent pieces sends them back to start. Bear off all seven pieces to win. Rules reconstructed from 4,500-year-old clay tablets.

games.title: Senet
games.tagline: Ancient Egyptian race game (c. 3500 BCE), reconstructed from archaeological evidence
games.how_to_play: Race five pieces along a 30-square winding path. Throw four sticks for movement. Capture opponent pieces by swapping positions. Special squares grant protection, send pieces backward, or require exact throws to bear off. Blockades of three or more pieces cannot be passed.

games.title: Shogi
games.tagline: Japan's classic strategy game where captured pieces change sides
games.how_to_play: Capture the opponent's King. Unique feature: captured pieces change allegiance and may be dropped back onto the board on any later turn. Most pieces promote upon reaching the opponent's territory, gaining new movement abilities.

variants.title: Standard Shogi
variants.special: Captured pieces become your own and can be dropped back onto the board

variants.title: Sho Shogi
variants.win: Checkmate, or capture both royal pieces if Crown Prince promoted
variants.special: 16th-century predecessor to modern Shogi. Adds the Drunken Elephant, which promotes to the Crown Prince — a second royal piece. No drop rule.

variants.title: Dobutsu Shogi
variants.win: Capture the enemy Lion, or move your Lion to the opponent's back rank without it being in immediate danger
variants.special: Animal-themed introductory Shogi on a 3×4 board, designed for young children. Invented by professional Shogi player Madoka Kitao. All pieces show their moves printed on the piece face. A solved game.

variants.title: Gorogoro+
variants.special: Shogi on a 5×6 board with no Bishop or Rook. Each player starts with a Knight and Lance in hand. Promotion in the last two ranks only.

variants.title: Tori Shogi
variants.special: Bird Shogi, invented 1799. 7×7 board, bird-themed pieces, drop rules. Only two pieces promote. Repetition caused by your own moves is a loss. One of the oldest Shogi variants with the drop rule.

variants.title: Cannon Shogi
variants.special: Shogi plus four Cannon types drawn from Xiangqi and Janggi, each with unique movement and capture rules. Pawns replaced with Janggi-style Soldiers. Invented by Peter Michaelsen, 1998.

variants.title: Annan Shogi
variants.special: Each piece borrows the movement of the friendly piece directly behind it. A Pawn backed by a Rook moves like a Rook.

variants.title: Chu Shogi
variants.win: Capture all opponent royal pieces (King and any Prince)
variants.special: Historical Japanese chess, dominant for centuries before modern Shogi. 46 pieces of 21 types per side on a 12×12 board. No drops. Features the powerful Lion (double-move, can capture twice) with special trading restrictions. Optional promotion to predetermined promoted forms in the far 4 ranks.

variants.title: Dai Shogi
variants.special: Historical Japanese 15×15 large Shogi variant; precursor to Chu Shogi. 65 pieces per side including Lion (double-mover), Kirin, Phoenix, and Drunk Elephant (promotes to Crown Prince, a second royal). No drops. Extinction royalty: player loses only when their last royal is captured.

variants.title: Four Player Shogi
variants.win: Checkmate both enemy Kings (team); or capture all other Kings (individual)
variants.special: 4-player Shogi on a cross-shaped board. Each player commands a standard Shogi army in one 3×9 wing. East and West players swap their Rook and Bishop starting positions. Drops apply with team restrictions. Three game styles: Team-Orthogonal, Team-Diagonal, and Individual. Michael Shipley, 1999.

variants.title: Hasami Shogi
variants.win: Reduce opponent to one remaining piece
variants.special: Custodial sandwich capture. No drops, no promotion. All pieces are identical.

variants.title: Heian Shogi
variants.win: Checkmate or bare the opponent's King
variants.special: The earliest reconstructed form of Japanese chess (~8th–9th century). 9×8 board, 18 pieces per side. No Rooks, no Bishops, no drops. All pieces promote to Gold General in the far 3 ranks. Win by checkmate or by baring the opponent's King.

variants.title: Hex Shogi 91
variants.special: 2-player Shogi variant on a 91-hexagon board (same shape as Glinski's Hexagonal Chess, differently oriented). All Shogi pieces adapted to hexagonal movement. Drops apply with hex-specific Pawn rules: no two-Pawn-per-file restriction (left out); Pawn drop may not check the King (stricter than Shogi). Promotion zone is 4 ranks. Fergus Duniho.

variants.title: Judkins' Shogi
variants.special: Modern miniature Shogi on a 6×6 board. 7 pieces per side. Includes drops. Promotion zone is the last 2 ranks. Rook promotes to Dragon, Bishop to Horse, Knight/Silver/Pawn promote to Gold.

variants.title: Kyoto Shogi
variants.special: Every piece except the King flips to its alternate face after each move

variants.title: Maka-Dai-Dai Shogi
variants.special: 19×19 historical Japanese Shogi variant meaning 'Great Dai-Dai Chess.' One of the largest chess-family games in recorded history. 96 pieces of 50 types per side (192 pieces total). No drops; captures remove permanently. Features Lion-power pieces, Hook Movers, the Emperor (universal leaper), and contagious promotion through the Teaching King and Buddhist Spirit. Promotion triggers on any capture. Historical; source: H. G. Muller (chessvariants.com).

variants.title: Minishogi
variants.special: Standard Shogi on a 5×5 board. Single-rank promotion zone. No Knights or Lances.

variants.title: Mortal Shogi
variants.special: Modern 9×9 Shogi variant by Roberto Lavieri and Fergus Duniho. Captured pieces demote one step in a fixed ranking chain (Dragon King → Dragon Horse → Rook → Bishop → Gold General → Silver General → Lance → Knight → removed) rather than returning to their original form. Promotes of sub-Gold pieces are flexible: any higher piece up to Gold General.

variants.title: Sankaku Shogi
variants.special: Modern Shogi variant on a 44-cell triangular board. 13 pieces per side: Emperor (leaps to any cell), Chariot (slides orthogonally, runs down Soldiers), Cavalry (leaps to second orthogonal), General (steps to any adjacent cell), and Soldiers. Captured pieces are removed permanently. Soldiers and Cavalry promote to General upon any capture.

variants.title: Tai Shogi
variants.win: Capture the King (and Crown Prince if present)
variants.special: 25×25 historical Japanese Shogi variant. Name means 'Grand Chess.' Approximately 177 piece types per side (354 pieces total) — the largest documented chess variant with complete, verified piece movements for every piece. No drops; captured pieces removed from play. Intermediate in scale between Maka-Dai-Dai Shogi (19×19) and Taikyoku Shogi (36×36). Documented in historical Japanese manuscripts.

variants.title: Taikyoku Shogi
variants.win: Capture the King and Crown Prince
variants.special: 36×36 historical Japanese Shogi variant meaning 'Ultimate Chess.' The largest chess variant ever documented. 402 pieces per side (804 total on 1,296 squares). Whether it was ever played to completion is disputed — a single game is estimated to require 10,000+ moves. Documented in a single known Japanese manuscript. L. Lynn Smith transcription; source: chessvariants.com.

variants.title: Tenjiku Shogi
variants.special: Medieval Japanese 16×16 Shogi variant derived from Chu Shogi. Introduces Fire Demons (burn all adjacent enemies after moving; passively burn enemies that move adjacent to them), hierarchical jumping generals, and Lion Hawk / Free Eagle double-movers. No drops. Extinction royalty.

variants.title: Wa Shogi
variants.special: Played on an 11×11 board with 23 pieces of 14 different types per side. All non-Pawn pieces are unique. Played historically without drops; modern play often adds drops. Promotion zone is the last 3 ranks; each piece has a fixed promoted form.

variants.title: Yari Shogi
variants.special: Invented by Christian Freeling, 1981. ‘Yari’ means lance. All unpromoted pieces except Pawns include a forward-Lance movement. Extreme forward orientation. Includes drops; unlike standard Shogi, Pawns may drop to give checkmate.

games.title: Standard 52-Card Deck
games.tagline: Every game a standard deck of cards can play
games.how_to_play: A standard French-suited deck supports 18 games spanning climbing, trick-taking, draw-and-discard, poker, pegging, banking, and solitaire families. Four suits (Spades, Hearts, Diamonds, Clubs), thirteen ranks per suit.

games.title: Standard Dice
games.tagline: Games built on standard six-sided dice
games.how_to_play: Standard six-sided dice support five games spanning press-your-luck, betting, bluffing, and category-scoring families. Roll, set aside combinations, and decide whether to bank or risk it all.

games.title: Starforged
games.tagline: A perilous journey through the Forge, guided by moves and oracle tables
games.how_to_play: Take on the role of spacefaring Ironsworn, bound to sworn vows. Roll action dice against challenge dice, manage momentum and condition meters, and consult oracle tables for creative prompts. Plays solo, cooperatively, or with a GM.

games.title: Stern-Halma
games.tagline: Race across the star board to claim the opposite point
games.how_to_play: Race ten pieces from one arm of a six-pointed star to the opposite arm. Move one step or jump over adjacent pieces (yours or opponents') to reach empty spaces beyond. Chain multiple jumps in one move. First player to fill the opposite arm wins.

variants.title: Standard 2-Player Stern-Halma
variants.win: Move all 10 pieces into the opposite arm
variants.special: Step or chain-hop in six directions. No capture. Jumped pieces remain.

variants.title: Standard 3-Player Stern-Halma
variants.win: Move all 10 pieces into the opposite arm
variants.special: Alternating arms used. Each player's goal is the arm directly opposite their start.

variants.title: Standard 4-Player Stern-Halma
variants.win: Move all 10 pieces into the opposite arm
variants.special: Four players use diagonal arms (NE, SE, SW, NW), leaving N and S empty.

variants.title: Standard 6-Player Stern-Halma
variants.win: Move all 10 pieces into the opposite arm
variants.special: All six arms occupied. Maximum interaction; every path crosses contested territory.

variants.title: Super Chinese Checkers
variants.win: Move all 10 pieces into the opposite arm
variants.special: Extended hop: pieces may jump multiple empty spaces in a line before and after clearing a hurdle.

games.title: Surakarta
games.tagline: The loop-capture game of Java: capture through the corner arcs
games.how_to_play: Move pieces one step in any direction. Capture by routing your path through one or more of the eight corner loop arcs that extend outside the grid boundary. First player to capture all twelve opponent pieces wins.

games.title: Tafl
games.tagline: King against the horde: asymmetric Norse strategy games of the Viking Age
games.how_to_play: Asymmetric Norse board game family. Defenders protect a King trying to reach safety. Attackers control a larger force trying to capture the King. Capture by surrounding enemy pieces on two opposite sides. Variants differ in board size, escape goals, and special rules.

games.title: Talisman Worlds
games.tagline: A new hex board every game of Talisman
games.how_to_play: Replaces the fixed Talisman board with 61 hexagonal tiles arranged in four concentric rings around a hidden ending tile. Every game has a completely different setup while keeping all characters, cards, and core rules intact.

games.title: The Landlord's Game
games.tagline: Elizabeth Magie's 1904 economic satire — five variants spanning the game's full history from patent to Prosperity
games.how_to_play: Roll dice and move around a 40-space board, buying properties and charging rent. Five historical variants from austere patent rules to the collective-win Prosperity mode where the poorest player must double their wealth.

variants.title: 1904 Original
variants.win: Complete 5 circuits with the highest total wealth (lots + cash + luxuries)
variants.special: The pure patent ruleset — no houses, no Chance cards, lot tickets drawn at start. The ur-game.

variants.title: 1906 Commercial Edition
variants.win: Most wealth at end of game — every Title Deed card and every house counts 100
variants.special: The first published edition. Adds houses, Chance cards, auctions, Speculation space, railroad monopoly pricing, and section rent doubling.

variants.title: Single Tax
variants.win: Collective — all players win when public ownership is complete and wages are maximised
variants.special: Magie's intended lesson: play mid-game by vote. Land rents fund public acquisition of utilities, railroads, and colleges. Wages rise progressively.

variants.title: Prosperity
variants.win: First player to accumulate $3,000 in cash
variants.special: Magie's 1932 patent. Chance cube on doubles, No Trespassing signs, Idle Land speculation, railroad jumps, improvement tags. A complete standalone game, not a variant of 1906.

variants.title: Monarch of the World
variants.win: Demonstration only — the landlord inevitably wins
variants.special: One player gets all land, others get all other advantages and $100 each. The landlord receives no wages. Proves Magie's thesis: the land monopolist is monarch of the world.

games.title: Xiangqi
games.tagline: Ancient Chinese chess: cannon fire, palace tactics, and the river divide
games.how_to_play: Ancient Chinese chess on a 9×10 grid with a river divide. Generals confined to palace squares. Cannons capture by jumping over exactly one piece. Flying General rule prevents opposing Generals from facing each other. Checkmate the opposing General to win.

variants.title: Standard Xiangqi
variants.special: Cannon captures by jumping a screen piece. Flying General rule. Stalemate is a loss.

variants.title: San-kwo-k'i
variants.special: Three Kingdoms 3-player Xiangqi on a hexagonal trisected board. Eliminating a General captures that player's entire army.

variants.title: Janggi
variants.special: Cannon must jump to both move and capture. No river. Bikjang draw rule. Passing always legal.

variants.title: Jieqi
variants.special: Xiangqi with hidden information: all pieces except the General start face-down and are revealed when they first move. A growing competitive variant in China and Vietnam. Also known as Dark Chess or Cờ Úhp.

variants.title: Manchu+
variants.special: Asymmetric Xiangqi variant from the Qing Dynasty. The Manchu side loses its Horses, second Chariot, and both Cannons, gaining a single Banner piece that combines Chariot, Cannon, and Horse movement.

variants.title: Minixiangqi
variants.special: Xiangqi condensed to a 7×7 board. No river, no Advisors or Elephants. Soldiers can move sideways from the start. Invented by Shigenobu Kusumoto, Osaka, 1973.

variants.title: Quang Trung Chess
variants.win: Checkmate the General, or advance a Pawn to the last rank where it cannot be immediately captured
variants.special: Vietnamese 10×10 variant with novel piece types. Pawns and General restricted to central files; advancing a Pawn to the last rank wins.

variants.title: Xiangqi 42
variants.win: Checkmate the General (standard Xiangqi win conditions)
variants.special: Compact Xiangqi on a 7×6 grid (42 intersections). No river, no Elephants — fast tactical play on a minimal board.

variants.title: Yáng Qí
variants.special: Western-influenced Xiangqi redesign with FIDE-style pieces plus Vaos (diagonal screen-capture). King may swap with adjacent pieces.
